questions.stem: The right-hand heart shows a thickened wall and septum with a smaller left-sided cavity compared with the normal heart on the left. What hemodynamic stress most commonly drives this remodeling pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pericardial effusion compressing the ventricle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic volume overload from mitral regurgitation

choices.label: E
choices.text: An acute myocardial infarction with wall thinning

explanation.summary: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, with a thickened wall and reduced cavity size, is the classic adaptation to chronic pressure overload; sarcomeres added in parallel increase wall thickness to normalize wall stress.
explanation.whyCorrect: Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, with a thickened wall and reduced cavity size, is the classic adaptation to chronic pressure overload; sarcomeres added in parallel increase wall thickness to normalize wall stress.

questions.stem: Compared with the normal heart, the right-hand heart shows all four chambers enlarged with a thinned ventricular wall. What is the principal functional consequence of this remodeling?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired relaxation with preserved ejection fraction

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased wall thickness raising diastolic filling pressures

explanation.summary: Dilated cardiomyopathy features four-chamber enlargement and wall thinning; the dilated, weakened ventricle contracts poorly, lowering stroke volume and ejection fraction, the hallmark of systolic heart failure.

questions.stem: This flow diagram begins with reduced LV contractility and traces the body's compensatory loops. What is the long-term detrimental consequence of these neurohormonal responses?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced sympathetic tone causing chronic bradycardia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive loss of circulating blood volume leading to dehydration

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sustained fluid retention and increased preload/afterload

explanation.summary: Falling cardiac output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system, boosting sodium/water reabsorption, venous pressure, preload and heart rate; while acutely supportive, chronic activation raises workload and volume overload, accelerating heart-failure progression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Falling cardiac output activates RAAS and the sympathetic system, boosting sodium/water reabsorption, venous pressure, preload and heart rate; while acutely supportive, chronic activation raises workload and volume overload, accelerating heart-failure progression.

questions.stem: In this pressure-volume loop, the shaded loop is shifted relative to the normal loop with a downward-shifted end-systolic pressure-volume relationship. What does this indicate about ventricular function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced contractility with a larger end-systolic volume and decreased stroke volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased stroke volume from enhanced preload reserve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired relaxation with a steep end-diastolic pressure curve and normal contractility

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal systolic function with isolated valvular regurgitation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased contractility with a smaller end-systolic volume

explanation.summary: A depressed ESPVR reflects reduced contractility; the ventricle empties less completely, end-systolic volume rises, and stroke volume falls, the hallmark of systolic (reduced ejection fraction) heart failure.

questions.stem: This pressure-volume loop shows a taller, narrower shaded loop with an upward-shifted end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship compared to normal. What mechanism does it illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enhanced compliance allowing greater diastolic filling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic volume overload with an enlarged end-diastolic volume

choices.label: D
choices.text: A stiff, poorly compliant ventricle that fills at higher pressures

choices.label: E
choices.text: A dilated ventricle with depressed contractility and low ejection fraction

explanation.summary: An elevated EDPVR indicates increased diastolic stiffness; the ventricle requires higher filling pressures for a given volume, so end-diastolic volume and stroke volume shrink, characterizing diastolic (preserved ejection fraction) heart failure.
explanation.whyCorrect: An elevated EDPVR indicates increased diastolic stiffness; the ventricle requires higher filling pressures for a given volume, so end-diastolic volume and stroke volume shrink, characterizing diastolic (preserved ejection fraction) heart failure.

questions.stem: The diagram links how sarcomeres are added (in parallel vs in series) to two remodeling patterns of the ventricle. Which pairing is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parallel addition thins the wall; series addition thickens it without chamber change

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both parallel and series addition produce concentric hypertrophy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sarcomeres added in parallel produce concentric hypertrophy; sarcomeres added in series produce eccentric hypertrophy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither pattern changes chamber geometry, only wall thickness

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sarcomeres in parallel produce eccentric hypertrophy; in series produce concentric hypertrophy

explanation.summary: Pressure overload adds sarcomeres in parallel, thickening the wall (concentric hypertrophy), whereas volume overload adds sarcomeres in series, lengthening myocytes and dilating the chamber (eccentric hypertrophy).
explanation.whyCorrect: Pressure overload adds sarcomeres in parallel, thickening the wall (concentric hypertrophy), whereas volume overload adds sarcomeres in series, lengthening myocytes and dilating the chamber (eccentric hypertrophy).

questions.stem: Using the wall-stress relationship shown (stress = P x r / 2h), how does the ventricle normalize wall stress in response to chronic pressure overload versus volume overload?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wall stress is independent of chamber radius, so only pressure matters

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pressure overload thickens the wall; volume overload increases radius, requiring added wall thickness to normalize stress

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both overloads reduce wall thickness to lower stress

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing wall thickness always raises wall stress

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pressure overload increases radius while volume overload thickens the wall

explanation.summary: By Laplace's law, wall stress rises with pressure and radius and falls with wall thickness. Pressure overload adds thickness (concentric), while volume overload dilates the chamber (eccentric); in both cases increasing h helps normalize wall stress.
explanation.whyCorrect: By Laplace's law, wall stress rises with pressure and radius and falls with wall thickness. Pressure overload adds thickness (concentric), while volume overload dilates the chamber (eccentric); in both cases increasing h helps normalize wall stress.

questions.stem: On this curve relating stroke volume to ventricular end-diastolic volume, sarcomere cartoons show stretch increasing until a plateau. What accounts for the rising portion of the curve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sympathetic stimulation directly raises contractility independent of filling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Coronary vasodilation increases oxygen delivery to myocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greater diastolic stretch improves actin-myosin overlap

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced afterload allows more complete emptying

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased heart rate shortens filling time and raises output

explanation.summary: The Frank-Starling mechanism: increasing end-diastolic volume stretches sarcomeres toward their optimal length, enhancing cross-bridge overlap and contractile force; beyond the optimum (or with LV dysfunction) the curve plateaus or declines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Frank-Starling mechanism: increasing end-diastolic volume stretches sarcomeres toward their optimal length, enhancing cross-bridge overlap and contractile force; beyond the optimum (or with LV dysfunction) the curve plateaus or declines.

questions.stem: This patient has a markedly distended abdomen with a tense, fluid-filled contour and dilated superficial veins. In the context of fluid overload, what does this most likely represent?

explanation.summary: Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid within the peritoneal cavity, most often from portal hypertension (cirrhosis) or heart failure. The tense distension and visible collateral veins reflect the same imbalance in Starling forces and sodium retention that drives peripheral edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ascites is the pathological accumulation of fluid within the peritoneal cavity, most often from portal hypertension (cirrhosis) or heart failure. The tense distension and visible collateral veins reflect the same imbalance in Starling forces and sodium retention that drives peripheral edema.

questions.stem: In the left panel a fingertip has been pressed into this swollen lower leg, leaving a persistent indentation seen in the right panel. What physical finding does this demonstrate?

explanation.summary: Pressure that displaces interstitial fluid and leaves a lingering pit indicates pitting edema, typical of fluid overload from heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, or venous insufficiency. Non-pitting swelling (myxedema, chronic lymphedema) does not retain the indentation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pressure that displaces interstitial fluid and leaves a lingering pit indicates pitting edema, typical of fluid overload from heart failure, hypoalbuminemia, or venous insufficiency. Non-pitting swelling (myxedema, chronic lymphedema) does not retain the indentation.

questions.stem: This capillary-bed schematic maps the Starling forces and disease processes that cause edema. Through what direct effect does an increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure promote edema?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reduces capillary wall permeability to plasma proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: It increases lymphatic drainage of the interstitial space

choices.label: C
choices.text: It raises plasma oncotic pressure, pulling fluid back into the capillary

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shifts fluid from the interstitium into the intracellular compartment

choices.label: E
choices.text: It increases the outward force driving fluid from the capillary

explanation.summary: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out of the vessel. When it rises (e.g., in heart failure, venous obstruction, or cirrhosis) the outward filtration exceeds reabsorption and lymphatic clearance, so fluid accumulates in the interstitium as edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out of the vessel. When it rises (e.g., in heart failure, venous obstruction, or cirrhosis) the outward filtration exceeds reabsorption and lymphatic clearance, so fluid accumulates in the interstitium as edema.

questions.stem: This diagram partitions a 70 kg body into total body water and non-water mass, then subdivides body water into extracellular and intracellular fractions. Which fluid compartment holds the largest volume of water?

explanation.summary: Total body water is about 60% of body mass. Two-thirds of it is intracellular (~28 L in a 70 kg person) and one-third extracellular; the extracellular fraction is further split into interstitial fluid (~75%) and plasma (~25%), so the ICF is by far the largest single compartment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Total body water is about 60% of body mass. Two-thirds of it is intracellular (~28 L in a 70 kg person) and one-third extracellular; the extracellular fraction is further split into interstitial fluid (~75%) and plasma (~25%), so the ICF is by far the largest single compartment.

questions.stem: This diagram shows four arrows acting across a capillary wall, labeled Pc, Pi, and the oncotic pressures. Which of these forces favors movement of fluid OUT of the capillary into the interstitium?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interstitial oncotic pressure acting to reabsorb fluid

explanation.summary: By Starling's principle, capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) is the dominant force pushing fluid out of the vessel, while plasma (capillary) oncotic pressure pulls fluid back in. Net filtration reflects the balance of these opposing hydrostatic and oncotic forces.
explanation.whyCorrect: By Starling's principle, capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) is the dominant force pushing fluid out of the vessel, while plasma (capillary) oncotic pressure pulls fluid back in. Net filtration reflects the balance of these opposing hydrostatic and oncotic forces.

questions.stem: This microcirculation schematic shows an arteriole feeding a capillary bed that drains into a venule, alongside a separate network of green lymphatic capillaries. What is the principal function of that green lymphatic network?

choices.label: B
choices.text: To directly connect arterioles to venules, bypassing the capillaries

choices.label: C
choices.text: To secrete plasma proteins into the interstitium

choices.label: D
choices.text: To deliver oxygenated blood to the capillary bed

choices.label: E
choices.text: To generate the capillary hydrostatic pressure that drives filtration

explanation.summary: Lymphatic capillaries drain the small excess of fluid and protein that filters out of the blood capillaries into the interstitium, returning it to the venous system. When lymphatic drainage is overwhelmed or obstructed, that fluid accumulates as edema.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphatic capillaries drain the small excess of fluid and protein that filters out of the blood capillaries into the interstitium, returning it to the venous system. When lymphatic drainage is overwhelmed or obstructed, that fluid accumulates as edema.

questions.stem: The 12-lead ECG shows tall R waves over the lateral/left-sided leads with a leftward-directed depolarization vector. What does this pattern indicate?

explanation.summary: Increased left ventricular muscle mass amplifies the leftward QRS vector, producing tall R waves in leads I, aVL, and V5-V6 with deep S waves in V1-V2, the hallmark of LVH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increased left ventricular muscle mass amplifies the leftward QRS vector, producing tall R waves in leads I, aVL, and V5-V6 with deep S waves in V1-V2, the hallmark of LVH.

questions.stem: This membrane diagram shows a drug blocking the Na+/K+-ATPase, after which intracellular Na+ rises, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger extrudes less Ca2+, and free intracellular Ca2+ increases to act on the myofibrils. What is the net effect of this sequence on the cardiac myocyte?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased contractility due to Ca2+ depletion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased contractility from higher intracellular Ca2+

choices.label: D
choices.text: Accelerated pacemaker firing at the SA node

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased extrusion of Ca2+ from the cell

explanation.summary: By inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase, the drug (digoxin) raises intracellular Na+, which reduces the driving gradient for the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. Less Ca2+ is pumped out, so intracellular Ca2+ accumulates and is available to the myofibrils, increasing contractile force (positive inotropy).
explanation.whyCorrect: By inhibiting the Na+/K+-ATPase, the drug (digoxin) raises intracellular Na+, which reduces the driving gradient for the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger. Less Ca2+ is pumped out, so intracellular Ca2+ accumulates and is available to the myofibrils, increasing contractile force (positive inotropy).
